Having spoken thus, Rama, his eyes flashing with anger, his 
lips compressed and trembling, tied fast his robe of bark and 
deerskin and knotted his hair, whereupon that sagacious One 
resembled Rudra bent upon the destruction of Tripura. 
Taking his bow from Lakshmana's hands, he drew it with 
might, selecting a terrible steel-pointed shafr resembling a 
venomous serpent, and the effulgent Rama, filled with wrath, 
the Scourge of his Foes, resembling the Fite at the destruction 
of the world, said :-
"As beings cannot escape old age, destiny or death, so is 
none able to restrain my wrath ! 0 Lakshmana, if I do not 
recover Sita this day in all her pristine beauty, I sball destroy 
the universe with its Gods, Gandharvas, human beings, 
Punnagas and mountains." 
CHAPTER 65 
Laluhmana seeks to pacify Rama 
A PRI!Y to grief on account of Sita's abduction, Rama, resembling 
the Fire of Dissolution, sought to bring about the destruction 
of the Worlds. 
With burning sighs he contemplated the stringed bow, as 
Hara at the end of the world-cycle stands ready to consume 
the universe. 
Seeing Rama transported with rage, hitherto never manifested 
by him, Lakshmana, his features pale with terror, addressed him 
with joined palms, saying :-
"Formerly thou wert ever gentle, of controlled mind and 
devoted to the welfare of all beings, do not now give way to 
wrath and renounce thy true nature. As the radiance of the 
moon, the brilliance of the sun, the velocity of the wind and 
the forbearance of the earth, so is thy glory manifested without 
equal and without end. Wherefore dost thou seek to destroy 
the worlds on account of one man's sin ?

brief.summary_1line: Rama, enraged by Sita’s abduction, vows to destroy the universe, but Lakshmana respectfully pleads with him to restrain his wrath.

image_candidates.scene_text: Rama, eyes blazing and hair knotted, draws a deadly arrow on his bow like Rudra preparing to destroy the universe.
Lakshmana stands with joined palms before the furious Rama, pale with fear as the warrior contemplates unleashing destruction.

deep.rich_summary: Rama, devastated by Sita’s abduction, erupts into a cosmic fury. Declaring that if he does not recover her he will unleash every weapon of destruction, he prepares himself like a god of annihilation—tightening his bark garments, taking up his bow, and resembling Rudra poised to destroy the triple cities. His wrath grows so immense that he threatens to destroy the entire universe—gods, spirits, humans, serpents, and mountains alike. Lakshmana, terrified at seeing a rage never before shown by his brother, steps forward with folded hands to restrain him. He reminds Rama of his true nature: gentle, self-controlled, and devoted to the welfare of all beings. Lakshmana argues that the sin of a single wrongdoer should not lead to the destruction of the worlds, appealing to Rama’s divine restraint and moral greatness.

highlight_spans.why: Rama’s grief-fueled vow to devastate the universe if Sita is not found sets the emotional and apocalyptic tone.
The comparison of Rama to Rudra destroying Tripura frames his anger in mythic, divine terms.
Rama’s explicit threat to destroy the entire cosmos—gods, beings, and mountains—marks the chapter’s pivotal dramatic escalation.
Lakshmana’s plea recalls Rama’s true nature—gentle, self-controlled, and cosmic in virtue—introducing the moral counterpoint to wrath.

top_scenes.scene_text: Rama, blazing with anger, tightens his bark garments and draws a serpent-like arrow while standing like Rudra poised to destroy the universe.
Lakshmana, pale with fear and hands folded, pleads before the wrathful Rama who stands with drawn bow like the fire of cosmic dissolution.
